object_types.name: Incident
object_types.definition: A formally declared problem or outage event triggered by an alert or customer report, identified by an incident number and tracked through states from triage to closure.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.
Unique. And we never delete incidents, which becomes relevant later.

object_types.name: IncidentNumber
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for an incident in the format INC- followed by a sequence number.

source_references.excerpt: Incident number. INC-, then a sequence.

object_types.name: IncidentSeverity
object_types.definition: A classification of incident blast radius and technical impact, ranging from SEV1 (everything down for everyone) to SEV4 (degraded, cosmetic, limited scope).

source_references.excerpt: SEV1 through SEV4. It's about blast radius and technical impact. SEV1 is everything's down for everyone. SEV4 is degraded, cosmetic, one region, nobody's really suffering.

object_types.name: IncidentPriority
object_types.definition: A classification of customer urgency and business impact, independent from severity, ranging from P1 (highest urgency) to P4 (lowest urgency).

source_references.excerpt: And priority is P1 through P4.
Priority is about customer urgency. Who's affected, what they've promised their own customers, whether we're breaching an SLA.

object_types.name: IncidentState
object_types.definition: The current lifecycle state of an incident: triage (initial assessment, no commander), declared (formally declared with commander assigned), mitigated (fix applied, monitoring in progress), resolved (confirmed fixed), or closed (incident lifecycle complete).

source_references.excerpt: Triage, declared, mitigated, resolved, closed.
Exactly one at a time.

object_types.name: Alert
object_types.definition: An automated or manually-raised alert from the monitoring platform that triggers or contributes to an incident.

source_references.excerpt: Monitoring fires an alert, or a customer tells us.
Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: AlertId
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for an alert, generated by the monitoring platform.

source_references.excerpt: Alert ID. Comes from the monitoring platform.

object_types.name: Ticket
object_types.definition: A customer support ticket that may be associated with an incident.

source_references.excerpt: the alert fires and support gets three tickets in the same two minutes.
And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: TicketNumber
object_types.definition: A unique identifier for a support ticket from the ticketing system.

source_references.excerpt: And a ticket has a ticket number. Different system, different format, always has.

object_types.name: Service
object_types.definition: A system or service offering owned by a team, which may be affected by an incident.

inferred_constraints.description: An incident cannot be a duplicate of itself.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: Can an incident be a duplicate of itself? Kit: ...That's a strange question. No, obviously not. I ask because if I write down "an incident is a duplicate of an incident" without saying so, that's permitted, and someone will eventually do it by accident. Nadia: Someone did do it by accident. There was a script. ... Facilitator: Then it's worth stating. An incident cannot be a duplicate of itself.

inferred_constraints.description: Duplicate relationships must not form chains or cycles. If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point directly to A, not to B.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: Can a chain form? B duplicates A, C duplicates B? Kit: It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. Facilitator: Is a chain wrong, or just untidy? Kit: It's wrong. If C duplicates B and B duplicates A, then C should point at A. When we roll up incident counts we only follow one hop, so a chain undercounts. Facilitator: So duplicates should point directly at a primary, and a primary is not itself a duplicate of anything. Kit: That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Severity and priority are stated as independent, but the model does not capture any explicit business rule about their relationship or lack thereof. The conversation mentions they can vary independently (e.g., SEV1 with P4), but whether there are any implicit constraints (e.g., certain combinations forbidden) is not discussed.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: Are they correlated at all? Owen: A P1 is always a SEV1. Nadia: That is not true. ... Facilitator: The point stands either way -- they're independent.

ambiguities.description: Incident commander optionality is clarified for declared vs. triage states, but the model does not distinguish state-dependent optionality in the constraint structure. The subset constraint models that only declared incidents can have commanders, but the data model should ideally reflect that a declared incident MUST have a commander. Currently, the internal_uniqueness constraint on 'Incident is commanded by Person' states 'at most one', but the mandatory constraint for declared incidents is not explicitly captured in ORM terms.

source_references.excerpt: An incident starts in triage. In triage there's no commander. A commander is assigned when it's declared. Declared incidents have exactly one commander. Triage incidents have none.

ambiguities.description: The duplicate relationship has an acyclic ring constraint to prevent chains, but the enforcement mechanism is not in place. The conversation explicitly states 'It's not enforced' and mentions a past incident where a script linked an incident to itself. The model captures the intended rule but should note that it is currently unenforceable.

source_references.excerpt: Kit: It shouldn't. The intent is that everything points at the primary directly. But nothing stops you making a chain and I've seen two-deep ones. ... Kit: That's the rule as intended. It's not enforced.

ambiguities.description: Severity changes over time are mentioned as happening in a timeline, but the model captures only the current severity as an attribute. Historical tracking of severity changes is not explicitly part of the conceptual model, only noted as a feature of the timeline.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: Constantly. Severity gets revised as we understand the blast radius. That's normal and expected. Facilitator: Is the history of that kept? Nadia: In the timeline, as events. The incident record carries the current severity.

ambiguities.description: The conversation discusses a potential future decision (whether to classify customer-caused incidents differently) but explicitly states this is undecided and will be escalated to Ravi. The model does not include any concept of incident cause classification because it does not yet exist.

source_references.excerpt: Facilitator: Is there a decision here today? Kit: No, and it's above all three of us. That's a decision about what we report to the board, and Ravi owns that. ... Facilitator: Parking it explicitly, then. Whether an incident later found to be caused by customer misconfiguration should be reclassified, excluded from reliability metrics, or left as-is, is undecided. The model today captures the five states and does not include any concept of a cause classification, because there isn't one to capture.

ambiguities.description: The relationship between incidents and their origins (alerts and tickets) allows an incident to have multiple origins, but the model does not explicitly distinguish between a manually-raised alert (created when an engineer spots something) and a monitoring-generated alert. The conversation mentions that a manual alert is still an alert and still requires a form link, but the model does not differentiate alert types.

source_references.excerpt: An engineer's looking at a dashboard for another reason and spots something. ...No, actually, let me correct that. If an engineer spots something, they raise it, and raising it creates an alert record. It's a manual alert but it's still an alert.
